author: NewsBreak
title: The Washburn Historic District in North Carolina includes rich family history of the Washburns - NewsBreak
text:
1 hours ago Photo by Washburn's General Store via Facebook. The historic Washburn General Store at 2426 Bostic Sunshine Highway in Bostic, North Carolina, is said to be the oldest continually-run family owned and operated retail business in the state of North Carolina. It's a fifth generation owned store that originally opened as a tavern in 1831 in Rutherford County on the Lincoln-Rutherford counties stagecoach line by Benjamin Washburn (1806-1863) .
The building was handed down to a past owner, the great-great nephew , Edward Nollie Washburn III (1930-2018) . In 2002, the general store, family mansion, barn (1915), and other buildings were designated as a historic district.
The buildings and area of about 63 acres represent the growth and maintenance carried on by the generations of the Washburn family since 1914.
On February 20, 2002, the Washburn Historic District was added to the U.S. National Register of Historic Places . There was a boundary increase of the historic district on January 25, 2006.
This historic district began to develop after 1915 and includes buildings featuring the Classical Revival architectural style. Some of the buildings included in the district are the Washburn-Davis House, the Washburn Funeral Home, and the Edgar Nollie Washburn House.
Washburn House (2013). Photo by Upstateherd, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons. The structures making up the historic district are located on Bostic-Sunshine Highway, Andrews Mill Road, and Salem Church Road. The historic district is in the community crossroads of Washburn, located about four miles from Bostic.
In 2002, when the store became part of the Washburn Historic District, it was owned by Ann Washburn Hutchins, daughter of Edward Nollie Washburn III. It's interesting the Washburn Historic District has buildings used by and lived in by generations of the Washburn family. This also includes the present generation.
The boundary increase on the National Register includes the Washburn-Davis house, which was built around 1905.
There's plenty of history associated with the Washburn family, which appears to have started with (Rev.) Reuben Washburn (1829-1904) , who was also the brother of Benjamin Washburn mentioned above. Earlier buildings housing the family and their commercial and agricultural businesses are gone.
Included in what's been lost was Reuben's two-story log house. He and his wife, Sarah Ann P. Crowder Washburn (1842-1910) , daughter, Bertha Locha Eunice Washburn (1886-1941), and a son lived in the house before Reuben passed away.
Later, Bertha built a farmhouse on land belonging to her family. The family lived there until Sarah Washburn died on November 16, 1910. According to the Find-a-Grave record, Reuben and Sarah had at least nine children.
According to deeds in 1902 , Reuben and Sarah, equally divided their lands between their surviving children, who each received a two-acre tract. Bertha was 16 at the time.
The National Register boundary increase in 2006 includes land conveyed to Bertha Washburn and her brother, John Lemuel Bascomb Washburn (1869-1937) . This land later came under the ownership of Daisy Tabitha Washburn Davis (1882-1961), who was another sibling.
Daisy's descendants had ownership at the time of the boundary increase for the National Register listing in 2006.
The lot conveyed to Bertha faced what's known today as Gun Club Road. It shared a north boundary with a two-acre house lot the Washburns conveyed to their son, Edgar Nollie Washburn Sr. (1874-1935) in 1899.
The house Edgar and his wife, Grace Harton Washburn (1883-1944), lived in is now lost. That's where they lived until building the large Colonial Revival brick house in 1914-1915.
Daisy Washburn received the two-acre lot belonging to the heirs of her brother, John Lemuel Bascomb Washburn. He also had another larger tract consisting of 30 or 35 acres bounded to the north by old Lincoln Road. It was being developed into a residential subdivision called Cobblestone, which is a neighborhood in Bostic.
The Washburn-Davis House is believed to have been built after Reuben died in 1904, and before Bertha married Elijah Hollifield (1874-1951) in 1909.
By late summer of 1910, sisters, Bertha and Daisy, wanted to exchange the two-acre lots received from their parents. In September 1910, Bertha sold the two-acre site to Daisy. In turn, in October 1910, Daisy sold her two-acre lot to Bertha.
Their mother, Sarah, died in November 1910, at age 67. Daisy bought her house that year. She and her husband, Charles Daniel Davis (1870-1936), had two daughters, Merle Holland Davis Umstead (1901-1988), and Norma Gwendolyn Davis Gold (1906-2001).
Of note, Merle Davis Umstead was the wife of Governor William Bradley Umstead and the mother of Merle Bradley Umstead. Visit here to learn more about Mrs. Umstead's experience as First Lady of North Carolina.
Daisy and Charles Davis and their family lived in a community known as Sunshine north of the Washburn crossroads. This is also where Charles managed one of the Washburn family stores. It was known as the E. N. Washburn Store No. 2 and the Sunshine Cash Store .
After Sarah Washburn died, the house and adjoining 30 plus acres became rental property. Up until 1961 when Daisy died, the house and land were either rented together or separately.
In the summer of 1961, renovation of the historic home was completed. This represented the first substantial improvment of the house since it was built. After Daisy died, a 34.94-acre tract was inherited by her daughter, Merle Umstead.
After Merle Umstead died, her daughter, Merle B. Umstead Richey, inherited the tract. She was an attorney in Durham. In late 1995, she and her husband, Russell Earle Richey, joined in conveying the tract to Cherry Mountain Farms, LLC, which was a family entity entirely owned by the immediate family of Merle Umstead Richey.
There is rich family history associated with the Washburn Historic District.
Thanks for reading and sharing.
